title: CP bootstrapping experiments: TF notes and rotation scenarios
body:
Purpose:
This labbook captures a pragmatic, experiment-driven runbook for initial private control-plane (CP) bootstrapping, staged scaling experiments, and certificate/terraform-driven rotation procedures. It is intentionally operational and informal: notes, commands, heuristics and gotchas we saw during the Q3–Q4 onprem pilot. Use as a living reference when onboarding new clusters or designing upgrade windows for customers.

Scope and audience:
- Audience: field SREs, platform engineers, and solutions engineers doing customer onprem or VPC CP installs.
- Scope: initial seed cluster, TF module expectations, cluster-scale experiments (seed->10->50 nodes), KMS rotation, CA/cert rotation, and upgrade rollback runway planning.
- Not in scope: application node-level GPU ops (handled by infra/gpu team), detailed network provider configs.

Quick summary of recommended high-level flow:
1) Validate connectivity and account IAM (pre-checks)
2) Run tf bootstrap in dry-run and plan mode; assert state locking + remote backend reachable
3) Apply minimal core stack (etcd, control-plane-api, k8s primaries) with feature flags disabled
4) Wait for telemetry & certificate issuance, then smoke test control-plane API end-to-end
5) Apply policy modules (RBAC, network policies) and gradually enable autoscaler/worker-provisioning
6) Run scale experiments in waves with steady-state observation windows (30–60m)
7) For rotations/upgrades: run canary control-plane upgrade, rotate KMS/CA on the canary, observe for 1–3h, then roll forward or rollback

Prereqs (explicit checklist):
- TF remote state (s3/azblob/gcs) configured and reachable from deploy host
- State locking (dynamoDB/raft-compatible lock) enabled to avoid concurrent applies
- Access to KMS/HSM with temporary test keys for rotation rehearsals
- OIDC cert issuer access for control-plane (if customer uses internal CA workflow, verify CSR automation)
- Clear outage window communicated to customer + Slack channel with oncall + runbook link

Environment topology notes (what we used in the lab):
- 3 control-plane VMs (small start: 4 vCPU / 16GB RAM) behind a VIP LB for API; etcd co-located on same CP VMs with dedicated disks
- Worker pools (k3s/k8s) autoscaling via cluster-autoscaler + terraform-managed ASGs
- KMS in customer VPC (AWS KMS or HashiCorp HSM) with GRPC proxy to control-plane for signed tokens

Bootstrap sequence (concrete steps we ran during experiments):
A. Pre-check (local machine):
  - export TF_BACKEND_BUCKET=redwood-cp-test-state
  - terraform init -backend-config="bucket=$TF_BACKEND_BUCKET" -reconfigure
  - terraform plan -var-file=envs/staging.tfvars -out=plan.out
  - Check: plan.out doesn't include unexpected deletions of core modules

B. Minimal apply (core CP only):
  - terraform apply plan.out -target=module.cp_core -parallelism=10
  - Wait on: etcd membership healthy, api-server responding on /healthz, leader elected
  - smoke: curl -s -k https://$CP_LB:8443/healthz (expect 'ok')

C. Certificate & CSR flow validation:
  - Confirm the CA signer was created and cert-manager has issued node and component certs
  - Debug tip: cert-manager logs in the cert-manager namespace often show the CSR rejections; check permission scope of CSR service account

D. Enable worker pools and autoscaler (wave 1):
  - terraform apply -target=module.worker_pools -parallelism=8
  - Scale policy: bring workers from 0 -> 10 over 10 minutes, observe kube-apiserver response latency and etcd leader latency metrics

Terraform module notes and opinions (lessons learned):
- Keep core modules small and idempotent: module.cp_core should only touch certificates, etcd, api-service, and cluster-bootstrap secrets. Avoid coupling logging or metrics add-ons into cp_core.
- Use explicit resource naming rather than computed names to avoid drift when provider plugin versions change.
- Provide a dedicated small module for 'operator-rotation' that accepts an ordered list of components and exposes a "drain_and_restart" toggle; that lets oncall run a coordinated rotation via terraform apply -var='rotate=true' without hand-editing daemonsets.
- Version pinning: pin major provider versions in root tf and create a CHANGELOG.md for module inputs that will change provider semantics.
- Remote-exec: minimize remote-exec provisioners. When unavoidable, make them robust (retry loops + idempotent checks). We had a number of flakes when remote-exec depended on DNS propagation.

Scale experiments and observed heuristics (lab results):
- Small control-plane (3 x medium) handled up to 1500 QPS of control-plane API calls (list/watch churn from many small CRDs) for short bursts. For sustained >= 500 QPS increase etcd write contention and API latency rose after 40–50s under default etcd compaction windows.
- Recommendation: for workloads with high watch and small CRD churn, increase etcd cache sizes and tune keeper compaction frequency; keep an eye on proposal latency metric.
- Node rotation impact: rotating 10% of worker nodes at once produced <5% request latency bump for stateless workloads with appropriate pod disruption budgets; stateful workloads need staged rotations (5% waves).

Rotation and upgrade runway (detailed play):
1) Canary upgrade of control-plane API image and operator CRDs on a single CP node: use terraform -target to update one az/instance, or taint one cp VM (terraform taint module.cp_core.vm[0]) then apply.
2) Validate: api health, leader election, controller-manager logs for panics/mismatch, webhook admissions operational.
3) Perform KMS key rotation: create new key, update secrets encryption config, update cp components to reference new key, restart controllers in order (controllers -> api-server -> etcd as required).
4) Certificate CA rotation (offline procedure): create new CA, issue leaf certs, add new CA to trust bundle (dual trust), rotate leaf certs, remove old CA after observation window (recommended 24–72h depending on customer risk tolerance).

Rollback strategy (explicit):
- Always keep the last known-good terraform state snapshot (tag in remote state bucket and make a copy). For image upgrades keep last-good images available in ARTIFACT_REGISTRY.
- Rollback path for TF: terraform apply using the snapshot plan or revert git branch that triggered the apply and run terraform apply against that commit id.
- For certificate rollbacks: retain old keys for at least 72h and keep both trust roots active to avoid one-way trust failures.

Smoke tests and validation suite (what we run after each step):
- api-server health (3/3 cp nodes respond ok)
- kube-system pods are >= 95% ready in 10m window after change
- etcd cluster health (quorum, outstanding proposals queue length under threshold)
- example workloads: deploy a canary namespace with 5 replicas of a stateless service and run 5k synthetic requests over 10m
- metrics sanity: no sudden >2x spike in 95th percentile latency for apiserver or etcd

Common failure modes and diagnostic pointers:
- TF apply hung on remote backend: check network ACLs and S3/GCS permissions and validate lock table entry; sometimes previous CI run forgot to release lock.
- Cert-manager CSR stuck in Pending: verify signerPrincipal mapping and that the CSR approver pod has correct RBAC.
- Etcd snapshot restoration failed: confirm snapshot storage ACLs and that snapshots are taken from the same major version.

Open questions / TODOs (local experiments to run next):
- Test multi-region control-plane topologies for read-fallback and latency tradeoffs (specifically 3-region leaderless etcd test).
- Validate terraform provider upgrades (v4 -> v5) in isolated env and document breaking changes.
- Add a small "chaos" job to the lab to simulate transient network partitions during KMS rotation.

Appendix: example tf var snippet we used as a guardrail (paste-as-text):
variable "max_control_plane_change" {
  description = "Max number of control-plane nodes that terraform is allowed to replace in a single apply"
  type        = number
  default     = 1
}

Notes to future reader:
- This file intentionally mixes experiment logs with procedures. If you're doing a production rollout, extract the concrete steps into a customer-facing checklist and remove experimental artifacts.
- If you find a discrepancy between this doc and module README, prefer the module README but log a ticket so we reconcile.

Next steps before promoting to final runbook:
- Convert the smoke tests to an automated pipeline (ci/cp-smoke) and link it from the root module outputs.
- Author a short one-pager for customer SREs documenting expected maintenance windows and impact bands.
- Schedule a rotation rehearsal with one pilot customer during the next maintenance window.

End of labbook.
